analysis.one_liner: Bans imports of goods made with forced labor in China's Xinjiang region and sanctions those responsible.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 406–3 on September 22, 2020, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare all goods from China's Xinjiang region to be made with forced labor and bar them from U.S. ports unless Customs and Border Protection proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence. It would also sanction foreign individuals and companies that run or supply the forced-labor system, require State Department findings on genocide, and force companies listed on U.S. stock exchanges to disclose dealings tied to Xinjiang surveillance camps. The House passed it 406–3, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Uyghur, Kazakh, and Kyrgyz people subjected to forced labor in Xinjiang, whose exploitation would lose its U.S. market outlet; American workers and domestic producers who now compete against goods made at slave wages or no wages; and American investors, who would learn when companies they hold stock in deal with surveillance and camp operators. Under the bill's stated findings, as many as 1.8 million people have been detained in internment camps where detainees face forced labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forced-labor victims, U.S. workers, and investors

how_it_helps.text: It would ban all goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by workers in the region's 'poverty alleviation' and 'pairing-assistance' programs, from entering U.S. ports unless the Customs Commissioner personally finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that no forced labor was involved and reports that finding publicly.

It would require the President to annually list foreign people and companies that knowingly run or facilitate forced labor of Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang, then freeze their U.S. assets and bar them from entering the country, with only a narrow national-interest waiver.

It would require U.S.-listed companies to publicly disclose dealings with entities building mass surveillance systems or detention camps in Xinjiang or transacting with sanctioned human-rights abusers, and it would obligate the President to decide whether sanctions or criminal charges are warranted — designed to warn American investors of material risks in companies tied to the camps.

It would direct the Secretary of State to make a formal, public determination of whether the treatment of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities amounts to crimes against humanity or genocide, and to build a diplomatic strategy — with allies and through the UN — to end the practice, closing with the finding that as many as 1.8 million people have been held in internment camps.

It would direct the U.S. Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force to name the facilities and sectors — starting with cotton and tomatoes — that supply goods made with forced labor, and identify businesses selling those products in the United States, giving U.S. workers and honest importers a level playing field under the Tariff Act's existing ban on forced-labor imports.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. importers and retailers whose supply chains run through Xinjiang — especially apparel, textiles, tomato products, electronics, and solar inputs — would face blocked shipments, supply-chain upheaval, and sanctions or criminal exposure for knowingly using the forced-labor system. Consumers would likely pay somewhat higher prices for goods currently cheap because Xinjiang labor is coerced or unpaid. Companies with camp or surveillance ties would bear new disclosure costs and possible sanctions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Importers of Xinjiang-linked goods, and consumers

drawbacks.text: The import ban is sweeping: it presumes every product from Xinjiang involves forced labor, forcing companies to prove innocence with 'clear and convincing evidence' — a very high bar — which would disrupt legitimate supply chains and raise prices for U.S. consumers of cotton, tomato, and electronics goods.

The enforcement burden falls on Customs and Border Protection to verify supply chains in a region the bill itself says is impenetrable to honest auditing, because witnesses cannot speak freely amid government surveillance and officials have an incentive to conceal the forced-labor system.

The sanctions carry a presidential waiver 'in the national interest of the United States,' and enforcement for listed entities sunsets after five to eight years, so a future administration could soften the policy without a new act of Congress.

The securities disclosure requirement is riddled with carve-outs: it exempts from disclosure the very import of Xinjiang-made electronics, textiles, shoes, and food, so a company sourcing forced-labor cotton or textiles can avoid the disclosure that would trip an investigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — shutting the U.S. market to goods made by people held in internment camps — is large and directly advances the Tariff Act's century-old ban on forced-labor imports. The costs are real but manageable for a country that already runs Withhold Release Orders on Xinjiang cotton and computer parts; the bill's own audit-reliability finding is an argument that softer verification could not work. The weakest parts are the disclosure exemptions for textile and electronics imports and the presidential waiver, which a stricter Congress would have closed.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it near-unanimously, but the Senate referred it to its Foreign Relations Committee, never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McGovern introduced the bill on March 11, 2020, and it was referred to four House committees: Foreign Affairs, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Financial Services.
It drew 87 cosponsors — 64 of 231 House Democrats and 23 of 197 House Republicans — across party lines.

On September 22, 2020, the House passed the bill 406–3 under a suspension-of-the-rules vote, a fast-track procedure reserved for non-controversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority; Democrats voted 230–0, Republicans 176–2, and the lone independent voted no.
The Senate received the bill on September 23, 2020, and referred it to the Committee on Foreign Relations — and no further action ever appears in the record.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and every unpassed bill dies at that point; the Senate never voted on the version the House had passed 406–3.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers of Xinjiang-linked goods — apparel, tomato, electronics, and solar supply chains — and the Chinese entities running the forced-labor system were better off, because the U.S. market stayed open to their products and no sanctions, disclosure requirements, or import presumption ever took effect.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 230 of 231 Democrats and 176 of 198 Republicans voted yes, with only 3 no votes total.

industries.note: Xinjiang produces a large share of the world's cotton, and the bill would presume all Xinjiang-origin goods involve forced labor, forcing brands to rebuild supply chains or win a hard 'clear and convincing evidence' exemption from Customs. The U.S. had already issued Withhold Release Orders on Xinjiang cotton and garments, so the industry had notice the current model was at risk.

industries.industry: Chinese state-linked manufacturers in Xinjiang (including the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps)
industries.note: The bill would cut these entities off from U.S. ports, name them publicly in enforcement reports, and expose their officials to asset freezes and visa bans. Their business model — subsidized factories near internment camps paying little or nothing for detainee labor — depends on open Western markets.

industries.industry: U.S.-listed companies tied to Xinjiang surveillance and camps
industries.note: Companies doing business with builders of mass surveillance systems or detention camps would have to disclose those revenues in SEC filings, triggering a presidential decision on sanctions or criminal referral. The bill frames this as protecting American investors from material risks to share value and reputation.

industries.industry: Tomato and food processors sourcing from Xinjiang
industries.note: The bill names cotton and tomatoes as the first high-priority enforcement sectors, so food products with Xinjiang inputs would face the same import presumption as textiles.

industries.industry: U.S. domestic manufacturers competing with forced-labor imports
industries.note: Producers that follow U.S. labor law would no longer compete against goods made by detainees at a fraction of minimum wage or without compensation, a gap the State Department's Trafficking in Persons Report had documented.
